data.what_you_know: WorldCom (MCI WorldCom in 1999, later renamed MCI Inc. after it emerged from bankruptcy) committed one of the largest accounting frauds in US history. The SEC sued the company in 2002 (SEC v. WorldCom) and brought several Accounting and Auditing Enforcement Releases (AAERs) against executives, including CFO Scott Sullivan, Controller David Myers, Buford Yates and Betty Vinson. The SEC's amended complaint alleged that the company inflated its income from at least 1999 through the first quarter of 2002. In 1999-2000 the main tool was improper release of line-cost accruals and other reserves; in 2001-2002 it was capitalizing line costs. There were also 'top-side' revenue adjustments that began around 1999. The 2003 restatement, which ran to about $74-76B including goodwill write-downs, covered 2000-2001 and corrected earlier periods as well. The Beresford special committee report identified about $3.3B of improper reserve reductions starting in 1999. Fiscal 1999 is therefore within the misstated period, though the scale was smaller than in 2001.

data.reasoning_summary: This is a distressed off-price apparel retailer. data.reasoning_summary: This is a financially distressed off-price apparel retailer. However, the filing records sizable one-time charges, discloses estimates candidly, reports declining earnings without obvious smoothing, has a clean audit opinion and no auditor change, and shows no unusual revenue recognition, related-party or off-balance-sheet red flags. Overall the evidence is weak and the profile looks like an ordinary non-fraud retailer.

To the extent this time frame changes, additional charges may be recorded in the future from $1.4 million per year up to the net remaining obligation under the lease depending on the facts and circumstances in existence at the time. As of February 2, Year T, the aggregate net remaining obligation under this lease was approximately $7.5 million.

evidence.why: This covenant-pressure disclosure is new this year, after the company took on $25M of debt. Covenant pressure is a known incentive to manage earnings.

evidence.why: Executive pay is tied to EPS growth targets, which gives an incentive to hit them. Here, though, the targets were missed and the expense was reversed, which suggests earnings were not pushed up to meet them.

data.reasoning_summary: This is a mall-based teen apparel retailer that is growing fast while its comparable store sales decline. Margins compressed and SG&A rose because of disclosed one-time charges: a $4.2M equipment disposal and a $1.4M rent reserve. The main judgment areas are the inventory markdown estimate (inventory grew 23.9% against 16.2% sales growth with negative comps) and a rent reserve covering only one year of a $7.5M obligation. New debt covenants and EPS-based executive awards create some incentive to manage earnings. On the other side, the company took sizable charges, reversed EPS-linked compensation when targets were missed, explains its results in detail and with internal consistency, received a clean audit opinion and changed no accountants. Revenue recognition is simple point-of-sale. No specific sign of manipulation appears, and the filing looks like a typical non-fraud retailer under ordinary business stress.

data.what_you_know: Pacific Sunwear of California (PacSun) is a mall-based specialty retailer of casual apparel, footwear and accessories for teens and young adults, based in Anaheim, CA, which also ran the d.e.m.o. and One Thousand Steps concepts. In fiscal 2002 it was growing steadily, with comparable store sales and earnings rising. In early 2005 it restated for lease accounting (rent holidays, straight-line rent and tenant allowances), along with many other retailers after the SEC's February 2005 clarification letter. That was an industry-wide technical correction, not fraud. I do not recall any SEC enforcement action or AAER about PacSun's financial statements for fiscal 2002.

evidence.quote: Due primarily to a change in the deferred tax asset recorded for net operating loss carryforwards, the valuation allowance decreased by $1,913,000 in the year ended April 30, Year T
evidence.why: The profitability that triggers use of the NOLs comes from the same revenue surge. On its own this is a weak signal.

evidence.quote: $4.0 million in municipal bonds maturing after 20 years
evidence.why: MD&A says 20 years while Note 2 says 'after 10 years', and long-dated bonds are classified as short-term investments. This is a small inconsistency in disclosure quality and is not material.

evidence.quote: this note receivable is being forgiven at the rate of $25,000 per quarter, contingent upon the officer's continued employment with the Company.
evidence.why: A related-party loan to an officer that is being forgiven. The amount is immaterial, but it shows weak governance.

data.reasoning_summary: Shortly after its IPO, this small software company went from years of large losses to a $4.4M profit on 24% revenue growth. The growth came mostly from partner and distributor license sales, now 59% of license revenue, plus an unexpected rise in legacy client/server licenses. Operating cash flow was only $0.9M against $4.4M of net income. Receivables rose significantly, and fourth-quarter revenue was up $2.0M. Together these are classic warning signs of premature or channel-stuffed software license revenue recognition, a common fraud pattern in that era. Against this, cost control explains part of the profit (SG&A fell $1.2M), the auditor gave a clean opinion, no single customer exceeds 10% of revenue, and there are no restatements, auditor changes or unusual reserve releases. The excerpts leave out the actual financial statement tables, including the allowance schedule and DSO data, so the receivables build cannot be quantified. Overall risk is moderately elevated, centered on revenue recognition.

evidence.quote: This increase in operating cash flows was due primarily to improved profitability in fiscal Year T, offset by the effect of a significant increase in accounts receivable. Net income for fiscal Year T was $4.4 million as compared to net losses of $2.4 million and $11.8 million in fiscal Year T-1 and Year T-2, respectively.
evidence.why: A sharp swing from losses to $4.4M net income while operating cash flow was only $0.9M. The gap comes mostly from a significant rise in receivables, a classic sign of premature or fictitious revenue.

evidence.quote: The increase in accounts receivable at April 30, Year T as compared to April 30, Year T-1 was due in part to an increase of $2.0 million in total revenues in the fourth quarter of fiscal Year T over the same quarter of fiscal Year T-1.
evidence.why: Revenue is concentrated in the fourth quarter and only 'in part' explains the AR build-up. This fits pulling sales forward at year-end.

evidence.quote: Revenues from partners accounted for approximately 59%, 57% and 48% of the Company's software license revenues for fiscal Year T, Year T-1 and Year T-2, respectively.
evidence.why: License revenue relies more and more on distributors and partners. Channel sales carry higher risk of sell-in, side agreements and channel stuffing.

evidence.quote: Improved penetration of [COMPANY] VISION was particularly strong in vertical application partner accounts as a result of a renewed focus on those customers in fiscal Year T.
evidence.why: The 55% growth in Internet license revenue is credited to partner accounts, the riskiest channel for revenue recognition.

evidence.quote: The results for client/server products were better than expected in light of the age of these product lines
evidence.why: Legacy product revenue rose against a declining trend. Management itself flags this as unexpected.

evidence.why: The prior-year caution about the revenue recognition practices under SOP 97-2 was removed in the year revenue and profit jumped.

evidence.why: The company has a history of recognizing large license orders that were never collected, which suggests weak credit and revenue controls.

evidence.quote: This amount was recorded as a prepaid asset as the value of the distributor rights acquired and is being amortized as certain revenues are recorded.
evidence.why: Receivables from a related distributor were cancelled and turned into a capitalized asset instead of written off. This shows aggressive related-party accounting, though the amount is small.

evidence.why: Earnings benefit from NOL usage. This is consistent with genuine profitability but makes reported earnings depend on the revenue figures.

data.reasoning_summary: This is a small software company with a recent IPO, moving from heavy losses to a $4.4M profit on 24% revenue growth. The growth is driven by license sales through partners and distributors (59% of license revenue). Operating cash flow ($0.9M) lags net income badly because of a significant receivables build-up linked to fourth-quarter revenue. Legacy product revenue also beat expectations. The year-over-year comparison shows the prior caution about SOP 97-2 revenue practices was dropped, and the company has a history of recognizing uncollectible large license orders. Together these fit premature or channel-stuffed license revenue, the most common SEC software fraud pattern. Against this, there is a clean audit opinion and no auditor change in Year T. The cost cuts that explain much of the margin improvement are plausible, and the AR increase is disclosed openly. Overall the risk is moderately elevated.

data.what_you_know: Unify Corp (Sacramento-area database/software tools vendor, renamed Daegis Inc. in 2011) had a fiscal year ending April 30. In mid-2000 it disclosed accounting irregularities, fired CEO Reza Mikailli and CFO Gholamreza (Gary) Kadjar... (CFO), and restated results for fiscal 2000 quarters (ending July 1999, Oct 1999, Jan 2000) after improper revenue recognition: fictitious or contingent sales, side letters, and backdated contracts. Nasdaq halted trading. The SEC brought enforcement actions (with AAERs) around 2002 against the company and former executives, and there were criminal charges as well. Under the Compustat convention, an April 2000 year-end is labeled fiscal 1999, so this year very likely matches the misstated period. Some uncertainty: if 'fiscal 1999' means the year ended April 30, 1999, that year was less clearly part of the fraud.
